title: Introduction to DBMS
summary: Every app runs on a database. Learn what a DBMS is, why flat files fail, what ACID and data independence buy you, and when a database is the wrong tool.

blocks.markdown:
A **database** is organized data you can trust. A **DBMS** is the software that stores it, guards it, and answers questions about it fast.

Picture a cafe's receipts. In a shoebox, "all oat-milk orders in June" means reading every slip. A DBMS is the clerk who keeps them sorted, lets many baristas file at once, and never loses one — even on a crash.

- **Database** = the data. **DBMS** = the engine managing it (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB).
- You get **fast queries**, **concurrent** access, and **crash-safe** durability.
- It's the source of truth behind almost every app screen.

blocks.subTitle: Data vs database vs DBMS
blocks.markdown:
Three words people blur — interviewers love the mix-up.

| Term | What it is | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Data | Raw facts, no context | `"Latte"`, `4.50` |
| Database | Data organized for a purpose | an `orders` table |
| DBMS | Software that manages it | PostgreSQL on a server |

So **MySQL is a DBMS**; the tables inside it are **the database**; a single price is **data**. You talk to the DBMS; it reads and writes the database for you.

blocks.subTitle: The pain before databases
blocks.markdown:
Before databases, programs saved data in **flat files** each app read and wrote itself. Fine when tiny; at real scale it breaks the same ways every time:

- **Concurrency** — two programs writing at once **overwrite** each other. No referee.
- **No fast lookup** — finding one record means **scanning the whole file**.
- **Crash damage** — a crash mid-write leaves the file **half-updated and corrupt**.
- **Duplicated logic** — every app re-invents search, backup, and format code.

A DBMS fixes all four: **one engine** owns storage, safety, indexing, and access.

blocks.subTitle: DBMS vs plain files
blocks.markdown:
A DBMS buys guarantees a flat file cannot.

| Concern | Flat file | DBMS |
|---|---|---|
| Many writers | Silent corruption | Safe (locking / MVCC) |
| Find one record | Scan all — O(n) | Indexed — ~O(log n) |
| Crash mid-write | Data mangled | Recovered via log |
| Enforce a rule | Every app remembers | Declared once, always |

You trade a little setup for **correctness and speed at scale**. Below a few rarely-changing values, a plain file is genuinely fine.

blocks.subTitle: Worked example: the lost update
blocks.markdown:
Concurrency sounds abstract until it costs money. An account has **$100**; two withdrawals, **$60** and **$50**, hit at the same instant. On a flat file each does read → subtract → write:

```
P1 reads 100 ─┐
P2 reads 100 ─┤  both saw 100
P1 writes 40
P2 writes 50  ← overwrites P1
```

Final balance: **$50** — the bank gave away $60. That's a **lost update**: nothing stopped two writers seeing the same start value. In a DBMS, wrapping both in transactions makes the engine **serialize** them (locks or MVCC) — the second withdrawal correctly fails for insufficient funds.

blocks.subTitle: The core services
blocks.markdown:
Strip the buzzwords and a DBMS earns its keep with six services:

- **Querying** — ask anything in SQL without scanning everything.
- **Concurrency control** — many users read/write at once without corruption.
- **Data integrity** — declared rules (types, keys, `NOT NULL`) enforced on every write.
- **Crash recovery** — a write-ahead log restores a consistent state after a crash.
- **Security** — access control per table or column.
- **Shared access** — one store for every app.

The theme: **you declare intent; the DBMS handles the mechanics** you'd otherwise rewrite in every app.

blocks.subTitle: ACID in one breath
blocks.markdown:
The headline promise is **ACID** — the properties that make a **transaction** (a group of steps) behave as one reliable unit.

- **Atomicity** — all steps happen or none do; a half-done transfer rolls back.
- **Consistency** — declared rules (constraints, keys) hold at every boundary.
- **Isolation** — concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-finished work.
- **Durability** — once "committed", the data survives a crash (it was logged first).

Deep dive: [transactions-acid](transactions-acid).

blocks.subTitle: Data independence: change storage without breaking apps
blocks.markdown:
A subtle-but-huge benefit is **data independence** — apps talk to an abstract view, not to bytes on disk. Classic theory splits it into three levels:

| Level | Describes | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Physical | How bytes are stored | B-tree files, pages |
| Logical | Tables, columns, relations | `orders(id, user_id, total)` |
| View | What one app sees | a "my orders" view |

- **Physical independence** — add an index or change format, **no query changes**.
- **Logical independence** — add a column, and apps that ignore it keep working.

This is *why* a DBMS scales as teams grow: storage tunes the physical layer while product ships against a stable logical schema.

Databases come in families, each shaped for a data pattern. The four to know:

| Type | Shaped for | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Relational (SQL) | Structured rows, joins, ACID | PostgreSQL, MySQL |
| Document | Flexible, nested records | MongoDB |
| Key-value | Ultra-fast lookups by key | Redis |
| Graph | Densely connected data | Neo4j |

**Relational is the sensible default** — it fits the widest range of problems. Reach for another only when your data genuinely doesn't fit ([data-models](data-models)).

blocks.subTitle: SQL vs NoSQL, decided
blocks.markdown:
The split beginners always ask about — as a decision, not a rivalry.

| Dimension | SQL | NoSQL |
|---|---|---|
| Schema | Fixed, declared | Flexible / implicit |
| Scaling | Vertical first | Scales out horizontally |
| Consistency | Strong (ACID) | Often eventual |
| Joins | First-class | Limited — denormalize |

- **Pick SQL** for money, orders, inventory — correctness-critical, interrelated data.
- **Pick NoSQL** for feeds, sessions, caches — huge scale, simple access.

Not "new beats old"; different constraints. Many systems use **both** ([nosql-modern-databases](nosql-modern-databases)).

Different people touch a database at different layers:

- **DBA** — installs, tunes, backs up, and secures it; owns uptime.
- **Database designer** — models the tables, keys, and relationships.
- **Developer** — writes the queries the app runs.
- **End user** — never sees it; just taps the app.

At a big company these are separate teams. On a small team **one engineer wears all four hats** — which is why understanding the whole stack pays off.

blocks.subTitle: The main parts
blocks.markdown:
Under the hood, a DBMS is a few parts cooperating. Three matter most:

![Inside a DBMS: query processor, storage engine, and transaction manager](assets/dbms-architecture.svg)

- **Query processor** — parses SQL; the **optimizer** plans the cheapest path.
- **Storage engine** — reads/writes **pages**, caching hot ones in a **buffer pool**.
- **Transaction manager** — logs changes to a **WAL** before applying, so commits survive crashes.

assets.alt: Inside a DBMS: query processor, storage engine, and transaction manager

blocks.subTitle: The life of a query
blocks.markdown:
Trace `SELECT total FROM orders WHERE id = 42;`:

1. **Parse** — SQL becomes a syntax tree; names checked against the catalog.
2. **Optimize** — `id` has a primary-key index, so the planner picks an **index seek** over a full scan (millions of rows → a few page reads).
3. **Execute & fetch** — the storage engine serves the page from the **buffer pool** on a hit, else reads disk and caches it.
4. **Return** — the row streams back to the client.

A write adds one step: the change is flushed to the **WAL before commit is acknowledged** — that's what makes durability real.

blocks.subTitle: Databases you'll meet
blocks.markdown:
The names you'll actually meet:

- **PostgreSQL** — feature-rich relational default; safe for most new backends.
- **MySQL / MariaDB** — the other relational workhorse; everywhere in web stacks.
- **SQLite** — a whole database in one file, no server; ships inside apps and phones.
- **MongoDB** — the popular document store for JSON-shaped data.
- **Redis** — in-memory key-value store, mostly a **cache**.

Advice: **learn one relational DB deeply** (Postgres). Schemas, indexes, transactions, and query plans transfer to every other engine.

blocks.subTitle: A tiny taste of SQL
blocks.markdown:
You talk to a relational DBMS in **SQL** — define a table, add data, ask a question:

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id     INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  drink  TEXT    NOT NULL,
  price  REAL    CHECK (price >= 0)
);

INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'Latte', 4.50), (2, 'Espresso', 3.00);

SELECT drink, price FROM orders WHERE price < 4.00;
```

```
drink     | price
----------+------
Espresso  | 3.00
```

The DBMS **enforced your rules**: `NOT NULL` rejects a nameless drink, `CHECK` rejects a negative price — no app code. That's data integrity.

A full DBMS isn't always right. Skip it when its guarantees buy nothing:

- **A few config values** → a `.env` file or key-value store.
- **Single-process scratch data** → just use program memory.
- **Massive append-only events** → a log/stream system (Kafka).
- **Static content** → flat files + a build step.

Reach for a DBMS when data must **outlive the process**, be **shared**, and stay **correct** under concurrency. No to all three? The setup buys you nothing.

blocks.subTitle: Beginner misconceptions
blocks.markdown:
Misconceptions worth dropping early:

- **"A database is just a spreadsheet."** A sheet has no concurrency safety, enforced types, or crash recovery.
- **"SQL and MySQL are the same."** SQL is the *language*; MySQL is one *DBMS* that speaks it.
- **"NoSQL is always faster."** It trades guarantees for scale — not a free speed-up.
- **"The DBMS makes my data correct."** It enforces only the rules *you* declare; a bad schema stores garbage happily.

blocks.subTitle: Subtler traps
blocks.markdown:
Traps that bite once you're past the basics:

- **Trusting defaults for correctness.** No foreign keys or `CHECK`s means the engine enforces only what you declared, not what you meant.
- **"Schemaless" isn't schema-free.** The schema just moves into app code, where it's easier to get subtly wrong.
- **Indexes aren't free.** Each speeds reads but **slows every write** and costs storage — don't add one per column.
- **Ignoring the query plan.** `EXPLAIN` shows why a query is slow; beginners never look.

blocks.subTitle: What is a DBMS
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is a DBMS and why use one over flat files?**

A **DBMS** is software that stores, retrieves, and manages structured data for applications. Over flat files it gives you four things you'd otherwise rewrite everywhere: **concurrent-safe writes** (no corruption), **indexed queries** (no full scans), **crash recovery** (a write-ahead log), and **shared, secured access** to one source of truth. Files give storage; a DBMS gives storage *plus* correctness, speed, and safety.

**Testing:** that you see a DBMS as a bundle of guarantees, not just a place to put data.

blocks.subTitle: Database vs DBMS
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What's the difference between a database and a DBMS?**

A **database** is the organized data itself — the tables and rows. A **DBMS** is the engine that manages it: storage, querying, concurrency, recovery. PostgreSQL is a DBMS; the `orders` and `users` tables inside it are the database. You send requests to the DBMS; it reads and writes the database for you.

**Testing:** precise vocabulary — that you don't conflate the data with the engine.

blocks.subTitle: Advantages of a DBMS
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What are the main advantages of a DBMS?**

Grouped: **concurrency** + **shared access** solve *sharing*; **data integrity** + **crash recovery** solve *correctness*; **fast querying** (indexes + optimizer) solves *performance*; **security** solves *access*. The alternative — every app managing its own files — re-implements all of that, inconsistently. It doesn't scale.

**Testing:** whether you can organize benefits into themes, not just reel off a list.

blocks.subTitle: Explain ACID
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Explain ACID with an example.**

ACID = the guarantees of a transaction. A $50 transfer from A to B:

- **Atomicity** — both debit and credit happen, or neither.
- **Consistency** — declared rules hold; the total is preserved.
- **Isolation** — a concurrent transfer can't see A debited before B is credited.
- **Durability** — once committed, a crash can't undo it.

Delivered via transactions, locking/MVCC, and a write-ahead log. See [transactions-acid](transactions-acid).

**Testing:** that you can ground each letter in a concrete scenario, not just expand the acronym.

blocks.subTitle: How to choose SQL vs NoSQL
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you choose between SQL and NoSQL?**

Start from the data and the guarantees it needs. **SQL** when data is **interrelated** and **correctness is critical** (orders, payments) — you get joins, a fixed schema, ACID. **NoSQL** when you need **horizontal scale** with **simple access** (feeds, sessions, caches) and can accept eventual consistency. I ask: multi-row transactions? rich relationships? stable schema? Mostly yes → SQL. Massive, flat, read-simple → NoSQL. Real systems use **both**.

**Testing:** that you decide from requirements, not hype.

blocks.subTitle: Data independence
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is data independence and why does it matter?**

Apps depend on an **abstract schema**, not on how data is physically stored. **Physical independence** — add an index or change the on-disk format, no query changes. **Logical independence** — add a column or table, and unaffected apps keep working. It **decouples teams**: storage engineers tune the physical layer while product ships against a stable logical schema. The classic three levels: physical → logical → view.

**Testing:** whether you grasp the layering that lets storage evolve without breaking apps.

blocks.subTitle: When NOT to use a DBMS
blocks.markdown:
**Q: When would you NOT use a full DBMS?**

When its guarantees buy nothing: a **config file** for a few settings; **in-memory structures** for single-process scratch data; a **log/stream system** (Kafka) for massive append-only events; **flat files + a build step** for static content. The test: must the data *outlive the process*, be *shared*, and stay *correct under concurrency*? No to all three → a DBMS is pure overhead.

**Testing:** engineering judgment — recognizing when a tool is overkill.

blocks.subTitle: What happens when you run a query
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Walk me through what happens when you run a SELECT.**

Five stages. **Parse** — SQL becomes a validated syntax tree. **Optimize** — the planner picks the cheapest plan (an index seek over a full scan when the filter column is indexed). **Execute** — the executor requests pages. **Fetch** — the storage engine serves them from the **buffer pool** on a hit, else reads disk and caches. **Return** — rows stream back. A write also flushes to the **WAL before commit is acknowledged** — that's durability.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about *why* a given query is slow.
